1:
The chapter opens not with a new oracle but with a resumption, and the witnesses note at once both the manner of it and the man who speaks. The reformed John Gill renders the opening word "added," and pictures Elihu pausing a while to see whether Job would make any reply to what he had already said; perceiving that he had no inclination to do so, and having more upon his mind to deliver, he went on with his discourse. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the observation: whereas Elihu's three preceding speeches were each introduced by the formula "and Elihu answered," this fourth is introduced only as a continuation of the others, "in honour of the number three," so that the very syntax marks it as an appendix rather than a fresh reply.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the resumption a speaker begging the patience of his hearers, and Job's in particular: he has not said all that he has to say, but he will not detain them long. Henry lets Elihu plead his warrant — that he speaks "on God's behalf," as an advocate for God, and may therefore justly expect the ear of the court; those who sincerely appear in the cause of God, to plead for his honour and his ways, shall neither want instructions nor lose their cause. And Henry adds the caution that hangs over every such advocacy, that a man may pretend to speak on God's behalf who really speaks for himself.

That caution the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns into a summary of the whole chapter, borrowing Heath's outline: Elihu will lay before Job the impropriety of his behaviour toward God, maintain that the Almighty administers impartial justice, promise prosperity to the obedient and threaten the stubborn, and close with the proofs of God's power and wisdom drawn from the heavens and the earth. But the other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, will not let Elihu's professions pass unweighed. It is not easy, he says, to acquit Elihu of some of the very "arrogance" he was so ready to ascribe to Job; he professes a great zeal for God, yet it is hard to see that all his large professions are warranted. So the verse sets the two estimates side by side — Henry's advocate honestly pleading God's cause, and Ellicott's speaker not wholly free of the self-importance he condemns in others — and the reader is left to listen for both notes in the speech that follows.
2:
Elihu asks only a little more patience, and the witnesses linger over the odd Hebrew of the request. The reformed John Gill observes that the word rendered "suffer me" carries the signification of a crown; yet he will not take it, as some do, in the sense of surrounding — "stand about me," as though a crowd were gathering to hear — for that could not properly be said to a single hearer; rather, with Aben Ezra, he takes it in the sense of doing honour: "do me the honour of giving me thy presence a little longer, and hearing me out patiently." Elihu proposes brevity, Gill notes, precisely that he may be heard with patience, since he will not long trespass upon it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the whole strophe before us — "Suffer me a little, and I will inform thee, for there is something still to be said for Eloah" — and dwell on its texture of rare and borrowed words. The verb behind "suffer me" is the Aramaic katter, and this, they remark, appears to be the only instance of that word being taken up as Hebrew; "I will inform thee" is a poetic Aramaism; and the little word for "a little," a diminutive form after the Arabic, belongs elsewhere to the popular speech of Jerusalem but is here used poetically. The sense they draw out is that Job is to wait yet a while, for what may be said in vindication of God against his complaints and accusations is not yet exhausted — "there still are words in favour of Eloah."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same request as a plea for a patient hearing — "let me have your attendance, your attention, awhile longer, and I will speak but this once, as plainly and as much to the purpose as I can" — and finds Elihu's warrant in the nobility of his theme: he has a good cause and a fruitful subject, for those who have spoken ever so much on God's behalf may yet find more to be spoken. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the point plain and undecorated: "I have other proofs to allege in behalf of God's justice and providence." The verse, on all their readings, is a hinge of courtesy: Elihu neither commands nor presumes upon the attention he wants, but asks it as a favour, pleading not his own importance but the greatness of his subject — that there remains something still to be said on God's side. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the strangeness of the wording only underlines the modesty of the plea, a man craving one more hearing not for himself but for the vindication of Eloah, whose cause he is not yet done pleading.
3:
The promise to "fetch knowledge from afar" sends the witnesses in search of what the distance means, and they scatter in interesting directions. The reformed John Gill offers three: that Elihu will draw on the wisdom of former ages and foreign countries, as men travelled far to hear Solomon; or that he will fetch his knowledge from God himself, whose nature and perfections are high as heaven and whose works are far above men; or, best of all, that the words should be read "I will bring forth knowledge concerning him that is afar off" — that is, concerning God, who is on high. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "from afar" as meaning both remote antiquity and heaven: "I will show thee that all antiquity and experience are on my side," bringing proofs from the remotest ages and most distant countries that God is infinitely wise, powerful, and good. And Clarke points forward to where that far-fetched knowledge will land — in the omnipotence and eternity of God, and in his economy in the atmosphere, the dew and rain, the thunder and lightning, with which the chapter closes.

John Wesley, of the same wesleyan-arminian school, hears Elihu widening his brief: "I will not confine my discourse to thy particular case, but will justify God by declaring his great and glorious works of creation and providence, both in heaven and in earth, and his dealing with men in other parts and ages of the world." The far country, on this reading, is the whole theatre of nature and history, ransacked to vindicate the ways of God.

Against all this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets a dry question: is not this precisely what Bildad had said before him, when he bade Job inquire of the former age (ch. 8:8)? And yet, Ellicott adds, the teaching Elihu is about to give in v.6 is not very different from Bildad's either — a hint that the speaker's grand preface may promise more novelty than it delivers. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical witness, simply complete the couplet, rendering "and to my Creator will I ascribe right," the second half of the vow that governs the whole speech: whatever Elihu fetches from afar, its end is to justify God. The witnesses converge on that purpose even as they differ over the distance; the knowledge may come from the ancients, from the heavens, or from God himself, but it is all pressed into one service, the ascribing of righteousness to the Maker.
4:
The claim to speak nothing false runs on into a phrase that the witnesses cannot agree how to point — "he that is perfect in knowledge is with thee" — and the ambiguity becomes the whole interest of the verse. The reformed John Gill takes the first clause at its plain worth: Elihu would say nothing but the truth, with the utmost impartiality and sincerity, so that what he said might be depended on, truth spoken briefly and clearly on so weighty a subject as the righteousness of God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "for truly my words are not lies; one perfect in knowledge stands before thee," and take the perfect one to be Elihu himself, presenting his credentials to the man he is about to instruct.

But the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same words the other way, turning "with thee" into a compliment to Job: "the perfection of knowledge is with thee; thou art a sensible, well-informed man, and wilt be able to judge of what I say." And John Wesley, of the same school, tilts it toward God: "thou hast to do with a God of perfect knowledge, by whom all thy words and actions are weighed" — so that the "perfect in knowledge" is not the speaker at all but the Judge before whom both speaker and hearer stand.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays the difficulty bare. We may presume Elihu meant God, he says; but in the Authorized Version it looks very much as though he meant himself, and the Vulgate seems to take it so too — the more so since the same phrase returns later in the speech (ch. 37:16), where Elihu again speaks of "him that is perfect in knowledge," and there too the wording hovers between the divine and the human claimant. So the debate is real and unresolved: is the one "perfect in knowledge" God, whose omniscience weighs every word; Job, competent to judge the argument; or Elihu himself, vouching for his own sufficiency? The stakes are not small, for on the last reading the verse is the very self-assurance that Ellicott had already scented as arrogance, while on the first it is a humble appeal to the God of truth. The witnesses do not force the point to a decision; they leave the clause hanging, as the Hebrew leaves it, between a modest confidence in God and an immodest confidence in the man.
5:
"God is mighty, and despiseth not any," Elihu declares, and the witnesses read the paradox of a might that stoops. The reformed John Gill dwells first on the "behold" and the greatness it announces — God the most mighty, the Almighty, seen in creation and providence, making all things out of nothing and upholding them by the word of his power, and seen too in redemption, ransoming his people out of the hand of them that are stronger than they. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the wonder that such might should "despise not any": God does not think it below him to take notice of the meanest of his subjects, nor does poverty or obscurity set any at a distance from his favour. Men who are mighty, Henry observes, are apt to look with haughty disdain on those of no distinction; but God, infinitely mighty, humbles himself to take cognizance of the affairs of the meanest, and this is a good reason why we should honour all men. Job had thought himself and his cause slighted because God did not appear for him at once; "No," says Elihu through Henry, "God despises not any" — and because his wisdom and strength are incontestably infinite, the condescensions of his grace can be no diminution to him.

Over the disputed phrase the wesleyan-arminian voices divide the sense finely. Adam Clarke prefers the active reading, "he despiseth not any," meaning that God reproaches no man for his want of knowledge — if any man lack wisdom he may come to God, who giveth liberally and upbraideth not (Jas. 1:5) — and he sets this above the passive "he will not be despised." Of the closing words Clarke notes that God is "mighty in strength of heart," one who can never be terrified nor alarmed. John Wesley keeps the moral edge: God's greatness does not make him, as it does men, despise or oppress the meanest; and his strength being "guided by wisdom," he can do nothing unbecoming God or unjust to his creatures.

That pairing of might with wisdom is, for the witnesses, the heart of the verse: power without wisdom would be terror, and wisdom without power would be pity that cannot save, but in God the two are one, so that his strength is never arbitrary and his condescension never weak. The verse thus lays the foundation for all Elihu's vindication — a God great enough to be feared and good enough to be trusted, who overlooks none, whether in judgment or in grace.
6:
Elihu's God is a governor who makes a difference between men, and the witnesses read the verse as the first clause of that even-handed justice. The reformed John Gill guards the sense of "preserveth not the life of the wicked": God preserves the life of all men so long as they live, but not in the same way — the wicked he keeps only in the common course of providence, not with that special care he shows the righteous, whose lives are dear and precious to him; nor does he preserve notorious sinners to any great length, for such do not live out half their days. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch anchor the strophe and correct a natural mistake: the subject of the verses that follow is in no case the wicked but the righteous, those as susceptible to discipline as they have need of it — a pattern they compare throughout to Psalm 107, which offers many parallels to Elihu's speeches.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the couplet balanced. Adam Clarke: God "will not give life to the wicked," for all such forfeit life by their transgressions, but "justice will he give to the afflicted or humble," the poor of the second clause; John Wesley hears in that clause a promise — "he will certainly in his time deliver his oppressed ones."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a portrait of the righteous Governor. He gives no countenance to the greatest if they be bad: though the wicked man's life may be prolonged, it is not under any special care of providence but only its common protection, and his preservation is but a reservation for the day of wrath (Rom. 2:5). Job had complained that the wicked live, grow old, and are mighty in power; "No," Elihu answers through Henry, God seldom suffers them to become old, nor preserves them with that comfort and satisfaction which are indeed our life. And Henry adds the verse's brighter half: God is always ready to right those who are injured and to plead their cause, giving right to the poor and avenging their quarrel upon their persecutors, forcing them to make restitution; if men will not right the injured poor, God will. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as two sides of one equity — no false security for the wicked, and no final neglect of the wronged.
7:
From the poor wronged Elihu turns to the righteous watched, and the witnesses warm to the unbroken gaze the verse describes. The reformed John Gill multiplies the senses of the eye that never turns away: God's eyes of providence are on the righteous to supply their wants and defend them from their enemies, and his eyes of love and mercy are on them from everlasting, viewing them as righteous in his Son; these were set on them before time and continue on them in time, through all their afflictions, temptations, and desertions, and shall never be withdrawn, for nothing can separate them from the love of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes "the righteous" as the righteous man in the singular, comparing the God who dwells on high yet humbles himself to behold the lowly (Ps. 113:5-8).

Over the second clause the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke proposes a small but telling repair. The words, he thinks, should run "but with kings upon the throne shall he place them, and they shall be exalted for ever," moving the verb "he will establish them" up into the first clause to clear the sense; and for "for ever" he would even read "to victory" — "with kings upon the throne will he place them, and they shall triumph to victory," precisely the promise to him that overcometh, to sit with Christ in his throne (Rev. 3:21). John Wesley keeps the plainer note: God never ceases to care for and watch over the righteous, who continue exalted and are not cast down from their dignity, as the wicked commonly are.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both the honour and its rarity. Sometimes God prefers good people to places of trust and power, and it is mercy both to them — for his grace will arm them against the temptations of preferment and enable them to do good — and to those over whom they are set, since when the righteous bear rule the city rejoices. Yet because we do not often see good men made great in this world, Henry lifts the promise to its surest fulfilment: the honour to which the righteous shall rise when their Redeemer stands at the latter day upon the earth, when they shall be exalted for ever and shine forth as the sun. The witnesses do not divide over the eye that never turns; they differ only in how high they pitch the throne — Clarke and Henry reaching past earthly dignity to the crown of the world to come, while Gill and Wesley keep the comfort of a present, ceaseless watching.
8:
The righteous, so watched and exalted, are nonetheless sometimes seen in chains, and the witnesses insist that the fetters of this verse belong to them and not to the wicked. The reformed John Gill is emphatic against the Targum, which made these the bonds of the wicked: the bound here are the righteous of the foregoing verse, with whom the passage is closely knit; and the binding is to be taken not literally, of imprisonment for righteousness' sake, but figuratively, of afflictions, the chastenings and corrections for sin that the next clause makes plain. The design, Gill says, is to obviate an objection — that the afflicted cannot be the objects of God's love — and to show that the eye of God is still upon them, his heart still toward them, however severely he seems to use them, since he has gracious ends in all of it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw a fine distinction in the imagery: the "chains" of the first clause are meant literally and the "bands" of the second figuratively, the very pairing the Psalmist joins in the affliction and iron of Psalm 107:10 — again the psalm whose profile Elihu's speech so often follows. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the pastoral point uppermost. Adam Clarke: these fetters "are means which God uses, not of punishment, but of correction"; John Wesley reads them of the vicissitude of worldly affairs, whereby men are brought even from a throne into a prison, as has sometimes befallen.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lets the picture widen to every kind of trouble: to be bound in fetters is to be laid in prison as Joseph was, or held in the cords of any other affliction — confined by pain and sickness, hampered by poverty, bound in one's counsels, and, for all one's struggling, held long in the distress. This, Henry notes, was Job's own case, caught and kept fast in the cords of anguish; and the very naming of it prepares the reader for the merciful design that the following verses will unfold, in which the God who binds is shown to bind for good. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse is set here precisely to forestall despair — that the sight of a good man in irons proves nothing against the love of God, whose fetters, on his own children, are the instruments not of a jailer but of a Father.
9:
The first purpose of the fetters is disclosure, and the witnesses gather around the affliction that holds a mirror to the soul. The reformed John Gill reads "their work" both ways: the work they ought to have done and neglected — sins of omission, the forsaken duty of prayer or of God's ordinances, which the affliction, as in a glass, presents to their view; or the work they did and should not have done, their sins of commission, for sin too is a work, a work of the flesh at which men toil, and even in good men their own act and deed. Now God, Gill says, in the glass of affliction holds forth to them what they had not seen. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "then He declareth to them their doing, and their transgressions, that they have been vainglorious," making the sin exposed a species of pride.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the same nerve. Adam Clarke: God "shows them the exceeding sinfulness of sin," and the word rendered "that they have exceeded" he traces to a root meaning "they have strengthened themselves" — that is, they leaned on their own strength and did not trust the living God, and so would not help themselves when trouble came. John Wesley takes "their work" as their evil works, brought to sight by affliction, and "exceeded" as having greatly sinned by abusing their power and prosperity, a fault to which even good men are too prone.

Here the other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, states what he calls Elihu's special doctrine: that God shows them the true nature of their conduct and their transgressions, that they have behaved themselves proudly, and that his chastisements are therefore by way of discipline, to reform the future rather than to chastise the past. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already framed it so — three things God intends in afflicting his people, the first being to discover past sins and bring them to remembrance, showing the fact of sin, the fault of it, and the sinfulness of it, that they have exceeded and been beyond measure sinful, so that true penitents lay a load upon themselves and do not extenuate but aggravate their sins. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the rod is first of all a teacher, and its opening lesson is self-knowledge — a man shown, in the glass of his own suffering, the work of his own hands.
10:
Disclosure gives way to instruction, and the witnesses hear in the opened ear the very grace of the affliction. The reformed John Gill turns the phrase over: God opens the ear "to correction," to the rod and to him who appointed it, hearing its reproving voice for sin, its directing voice to duty, its commanding voice to return from iniquity; or "to instruction," for God's corrections of his people are instructions, whereby they learn more of their duty, and of the love and faithfulness and covenant of God, so that sometimes more is learned by an affliction than by a sermon. But the ear must first be opened, done at conversion by the mighty power of God; and when his people fall asleep and grow inattentive, this is one way he takes to rouse them — he speaks to them, as to Job, out of a whirlwind.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "He openeth their ear to warning," the discipline a warning meant to be heeded and obeyed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps it brief and warm: God "gives them to understand the reason why they are thus corrected, and commands them to return from those iniquities" that drew the affliction down. John Wesley, of the same school, glosses the opening as a work upon the will — God "inclines them to hearken to what he speaks by the rod."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had set this second among the ends of affliction: to dispose the heart to receive present instruction, for whom God chastens he teaches (Ps. 94:12), the affliction softening the wax that it may take the seal — yet not of itself, but by the grace of God working with it, for it is he who opens the ear and opens the heart, who has the key of David. And the third end follows in the verse's own command: to draw men off from iniquity for the future, a summons to have no more to do with sin, to turn from it with aversion and a resolution never to return. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the opened ear is no natural effect of pain — pain of itself hardens as often as it softens — but the fruit of a grace that turns the rod into a word, and the word into a call home. It is the same lesson Elihu had pressed throughout his speeches, that God speaks in more ways than one, and that the sharpest of his languages, affliction, is meant to be not merely felt but heard.
11:
The opened ear may yet be obeyed or refused, and this verse takes the happier branch, though not without a frank admission of difficulty. The reformed John Gill fixes what "obey and serve him" means here: not so much obedience to God's word, his law or gospel, as obedience to his rod — to "hear" it and him who appointed it, to hearken to its reproving and instructing and commanding voice, to humble oneself under the mighty hand of God and return from iniquity. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line "if they hear and yield, they pass their days in prosperity and their years in pleasure," taking the verb in the sense of doing another's will rather than of religious service, and noting the neutral word for the "pleasures" in which such years are spent.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns the strain between the promise and experience, but will not surrender it: there may appear in the course of providence to be some exceptions to this general rule, yet it is most true, literally or spiritually, of all the genuine followers of God, for every man is happy, in whatever circumstances, whose heart is unreservedly dedicated to his Maker. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the promise home as double: piety is the only sure way to prosperity and pleasure, for if we faithfully serve God we have the promise of the life that now is, so far as is for God's glory and our good — and who would desire it further? — and the possession of inward pleasures, the comfort of communion with God and the great peace of those who love his law.

Only the other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, lets the objection stand unanswered: it is perhaps not more easy to reconcile this teaching of Elihu's with the realities of actual fact than it is to reconcile the notions of Job's friends about direct retribution in this life. The verse thus carries its own quiet tension — a rule the witnesses believe and yet cannot always see, promising to the submissive a prosperity that the book of Job itself, in its hero's ash-heap, seems to put in question. The witnesses do not divide over the goodness of obedience; they differ only in candour, Clarke and Henry holding the promise fast while Ellicott marks how hard it is to square with the world as it is.
12:
The darker branch follows, and the witnesses read the ruin of the disobedient with an eye to the exact weapon named. The reformed John Gill sketches the man: one who seems righteous and is not, who when afflicted is not submissive but kicks against the pricks, rebels against God, complains and murmurs at his dealings. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "and if they hear not, they pass away by the bow and expire in lack of knowledge," making the instrument a shaft rather than a sword. And the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that the Hebrew behind "perish by the sword" is better "by a dart they shall pass by," or, as Mr. Good has it, "they pass by as an arrow" — a picture not of one decisive stroke but of men kept in continual danger, who often fall before they have lived out half their days; though he notes the Vulgate keeps the sword, "they shall pass away by the sword."

That the death is a death "without knowledge" the witnesses take in more than one key. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it doubly: they die "ere they are aware," without any further previous notice, cut off suddenly; or they die "because they were without knowledge," notwithstanding the means of knowledge they were blessed with — and those who die without knowledge die without grace and are undone for ever. Henry sets the whole under a solemn law: whom God's rod does not cure, his sword will kill, and the consuming fire will prevail if the refining fire do not, for when God judges he will overcome.

So the difference among the witnesses is one of image rather than substance. Whether the disobedient perish "by the sword" of the Authorized Version or "pass by as an arrow" with Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch, all read the verse as the strict counterpart of the promise before it: the same affliction that would have taught the submissive to prosper only hurries the rebellious, unwarned and unwise, out of the world. The witnesses do not finally divide; they weigh the exactness of the Hebrew weapon, and agree on the terror it carries — that to refuse the discipline of God is not to escape it but to meet it in its sharper form. And they agree, too, on the peculiar horror of the second clause: that such men die "without knowledge," ignorant to the last of the very thing their affliction was sent to teach them, so that the rod which might have been their schooling becomes, unheeded, their sentence.
13:
Elihu turns from those who refuse discipline to those who resent it, and the witnesses debate both who these are and whose wrath is heaped. The reformed John Gill takes them for the same disobedient men just named — those who seem righteous but are not, who have a double heart, drawing near with the mouth while the heart is far off. As to the heaping, he offers two ways: they "add" or increase the wrath of God, treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath; or, with Jarchi, the wrath is their own, for when afflictions come they reproach and blaspheme, are angry with God and quarrel at his dealings — "they put the nose," erecting it against him in pride. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch decide for the second: the wrath is not the divine anger but the impatience and murmuring of the man himself, who cherishes or harbours wrath in his heart, and who, being angry with God and not humbly praying to him, shows himself thereby one estranged from God and no righteous man.

Over the word "hypocrites" the witnesses part again. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will not have it: the Hebrew names the profligate and impious, those who have neither the form nor the power of godliness, whereas a hypocrite has the form without the power — and this, he insists, is not the meaning of the word in the book of Job. Charles Ellicott, of the grammatical-historical school, agrees that the words mean rather the godless or profane in heart; and he glosses "they cry not" as "cry not for help," and "when he bindeth them" as the same kind of affliction spoken of before, the binding in fetters like Joseph's. John Wesley keeps it simple — they cry not unto God for help, when he binds them with the cords of affliction.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the doctrine of hypocrisy out of it: hypocrisy lies in the heart, which is for the world and the flesh while the outside seems for God and religion, and its mischief is that hypocrites heap up wrath, doing daily what provokes God and treasuring it against the great day (Rom. 2:5). The witnesses thus circle two real questions — whether the "wrath" is God's, stored up against the impenitent, or the man's own, boiling against God; and whether the sinner here is the polished hypocrite or the open profligate — without wholly resolving either. What none of them doubts is the sign Elihu fastens on: not the affliction, but the silence under it, the man who will not cry when God binds him.
14:
The fate of the profane is a short life and a shameful company, and the witnesses work at both the "youth" and the "unclean." The reformed John Gill takes "their soul" for the whole person, and "die in youth" for a premature and untimely death — some few exceed the common term of life, multitudes never reach it, and these die before it. The word, he notes, signifies a violent shaking out, an "excussion," which the Vulgate renders "in a tempest" — a tempest of divine wrath and a storm in the conscience — while Jarchi interprets it of strangling. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "their soul dieth in the vigour of youth, and their life is like that of the unclean," and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke echoes the exactness: literally "they shall die in the youth of their soul," which is just the psalmist's word that bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days (Ps. 55:23).

Over "among the unclean" the witnesses split between this life and the next. Clarke fixes on the Hebrew word for the unclean, the qedeshim — the consecrated ones who in idolatry were the temple-prostitutes devoted to Baal and Ashtoreth, to Venus and Priapus — so that the profane "die among the unclean" as they lived, in the vilest company; Mr. Good renders it "the rabble," and the Septuagint turns it, "their life shall be wounded by the angels." John Wesley keeps the same earthly sense — Sodomites, to whose destruction Elihu may allude — but then carries it beyond death: after death their life is among the unclean spirits, the devil and his angels, for ever excluded from the new Jerusalem, into which no unclean thing shall enter.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole as the portion of hypocrites: they die a sudden death, in youth, when death is most a surprise, going to hell when they hoped for heaven; and they die the second death, their life after death among the unclean, the worst and vilest of sinners, the unclean spirits from whom the holy city is barred. So the genuine difference is over the register of the shame — Clarke and Wesley hearing first the earthly company of the qedeshim, Henry and Wesley pressing on to the unclean spirits of the world to come. The witnesses do not divide over the sentence itself: the profane heart that would not cry under the rod is cut off early and laid among the defiled, its brief life and its long death alike a warning.
15:
"He delivereth the poor in his affliction," Elihu says, and the little word "in" becomes the whole question of the verse. The reformed John Gill holds it fast: the poor here are the godly poor, humbled and made contrite through the afflicting hand, and the deliverance intended is not a rescue "out" of their affliction but a deliverance "in" it — God supporting them under it, supplying grace to bear it patiently, granting his presence for their comfort, stilling the enemy, and drawing their affections off the world to himself. Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the point differently: the drift of Elihu's discourse is rather that God "delivereth the afflicted by his affliction" — that he makes use of the very affliction as the means of deliverance, "and openeth their ears by oppression." Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, render it just so, "He delivereth the sufferer by his affliction, and openeth their ear by oppression," the trouble itself the instrument that saves.

The clause about the opened ear the witnesses read variously but warmly. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke suggests God "will let them know for what end they are afflicted"; but he offers a bolder rendering too — that the verb might be translated "he shall make them exult, or sing for joy, in oppression," like the three Hebrews who walked unhurt in the fiery furnace of Daniel 3. John Wesley keeps it obediential: God "causeth them to hear, and understand, and do, the will of God" in the day of oppression — the opened ear issuing not merely in knowledge but in obedience.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the comfort and turns it on Job. We all know how ready God is to deliver the poor in his affliction; the poor in spirit, the broken and contrite, he looks upon with tenderness, and even while he does not yet deliver them he opens their ears and speaks to them good and comfortable words, for the encouragement of their faith and the silencing of their fears. So the witnesses circle one genuine difference — whether God delivers the afflicted "in" their trouble, by upholding them within it, or "by" their trouble, using it as the very means of their rescue — and agree on the tenderness beneath both: that the God who binds is also the God who, in the binding, opens the ear and saves.
16:
Elihu now brings all his doctrine home to Job, and the witnesses divide over whether the verse looks back on a lost mercy or names a present one. The reformed John Gill takes it as Elihu accommodating what he has said to Job's own case: had Job hearkened to the voice of God in the rod, submitted to the chastening hand, and borne his affliction patiently, then thus it would have been with him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees flatly: "if thou hadst turned to, obeyed, and served him, thy present state would have been widely different from what it is," while John Wesley adds only that Job would have been brought "into a state of ease and freedom" had he opened his ear to God's counsels. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry spells the double blessing out: Job would have been enlarged, removed into a broad place where is no straitness, no longer cramped by his sickness and disgrace; and enriched, his table richly spread not only with food convenient but with the finest of the wheat and the fattest of the flesh (Deut. 32:14) — for it ought to silence us under affliction to consider that, if we were better, it would be every way better with us.

Against this whole conditional reading the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets an indicative one, and thinks the sense improved by it. Elihu may be speaking not of what God would have done but of what he has actually done: "yea, also he hath removed thee from the mouth of an adversary, even into ease and abundance where there was no straitness, and that which came down upon thy table was full of fatness" — God, in mercy, seeing Job in danger, removed the cause of temptation, and his chastisement would have been short had he been submissive; but he has been bold and daring, like the wicked, and so has reaped the judgment of the wicked.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, render the line "He bringeth thee out of the jaws of distress to a broad place, whose ground hath no straitness," and read it, like Ellicott, as the transition to the reproach that follows. So the debate is real: does the verse mourn a deliverance forfeited by Job's impatience, or record a deliverance God had already begun and Job had spoiled? On the picture itself the witnesses are one — a man drawn out of a strait place into room and plenty, a table heaped with fatness — and one too in its use: that the narrowness Job still suffers is not the measure of God's unwillingness but of his own unsubmissive heart.
17:
The reproach hinted at now falls, and the witnesses weigh how sharp it is meant to be. The reformed John Gill offers two constructions and leans to the graver. It might continue the happiness Job would have enjoyed — filled to satisfaction by seeing the judgments of God fall on the wicked who wronged him, on the Chaldeans and Sabeans, with judgment and justice upholding him; but the words rather express his present state and the reason of it, that he is not sufficiently humbled — not that he has lived a wicked man's life, but that in his impatience he has done as the wicked do. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "yet thou art become full of the judging of the evil-doer: judging and judgment lay hold on one another," a grim play on the word, as if the very act of judging others draws down judgment on the judge.

The wesleyan-arminian voices make the point moral rather than biographical. Adam Clarke: "as thou art acting like the wicked, so God deals with thee as he deals with them" — and he adds, with an honesty that recoils on himself, that none of Job's friends, Elihu included, knew anything of the permission God had given Satan to afflict an innocent man. John Wesley reads "the judgment of the wicked" as the sentence such men pass: Job has justified the hard speeches wicked men utter against God, maintained their cause against him, and so the just judgment of God, the condemnation due to the wicked, takes hold on him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sums it as Job standing in his own light and being the cause of the continuance of his own trouble: whatever he really is, in this thing he has conducted himself like a wicked man, has spoken and done like the wicked, has served their cause; and therefore, in Bishop Patrick's phrase, judgment and justice take hold on him as they would on any who keeps such company, for accessories to treason will be dealt with as principals. The witnesses do not divide over the charge's substance — that Job's fault lies not in his past life but in his present temper under the rod — though Gill weighs whether the verse describes a bliss forfeited or a judgment incurred. And Clarke's aside hangs over the whole, that Elihu, for all his zeal, is arraigning a man whose real cause neither he nor his fellows understood.
18:
A warning of wrath follows, and the witnesses first ask whose wrath is meant and then find one of their number reading the whole verse another way. The reformed John Gill weighs both: it may be wrath in Job — his impatience and heat under the afflicting hand, which Elihu bids him check, lest he provoke God to take him away at once; or, rather, wrath in God, his vindictive and punitive justice, revealed from heaven against all unrighteousness, of which the afflictions of even his own people are a lesser token, "a little wrath," which is no other than love displeased. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it of the times: this is a season when God is punishing the wicked, so "take heed lest thou be cut off in a moment — redeem the time, for the days are evil"; and when God determines to destroy, who can save? John Wesley keeps it personal — wrath conceived by God against Job, and if once it takes hold, no ransom will be accepted for him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as a friendly but necessary caution not to make light of divine vengeance: because God is a righteous governor who resents the affronts done to his government, Job has reason to fear his displeasure, and should make his peace quickly and get the anger turned away; even good men need to be kept to their duty by the fear of God's wrath, for the wisest and best have enough in them to deserve his stroke.

But the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch break with the whole line of it, and render the couplet "for let not anger indeed entice thee to scorning, and let not the greatness of the ransom mislead thee" — a warning not that no ransom can deliver Job, but that Job must not let his own anger seduce him into mockery, nor imagine that some great ransom might buy him off. Charles Ellicott meanwhile keeps nearer the received sense — "for there is wrath; beware lest he take thee away with one stroke, so that great ransom cannot deliver thee" — while noting that the Hebrew literally runs "let not a great ransom deliver thee." So a real difference opens beneath the verse: for most of the witnesses it threatens that no price can ransom a man once wrath has seized him, but for Keil and Delitzsch it warns Job against the temptation, in his anger, to think a ransom either needful or possible. The witnesses agree at least on the peril — that a man under the displeasure of God trifles with it at his soul's cost.
19:
The theme of a ransom that cannot buy off wrath runs into this verse, and the witnesses divide over whether it speaks of Job's wealth or Job's cry. The reformed John Gill reads riches: they can bear no weight with God, being his own to give and take, unable to ward off the stroke of death or profit in the day of wrath; Broughton would render it "will he esteem thy nobleness?" — thy rank and station among men — but God is no respecter of persons, and neither gold nor a fortress can bribe or bar him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the same sense, that all Job's riches, though he had as much as ever, and the strongest forces he could muster, would be nothing.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses the words doubtful and lays out the options: "will he esteem thy riches, that thou be not in distress?" or "all the forces of thy strength"; or else, taking the same consonants otherwise, "will thy cry avail, that thou be not in distress?" — though he allows there is authority for the Authorized Version. Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, decide for the cry: they render "shall thy crying place thee beyond distress, and all the efforts of strength?" — reading the disputed word not as riches but as a call for help, so that the question is whether any amount of outcry or exertion can lift Job out of his straits.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, keeping the received reading, presses it into a lesson on the vanity of every human refuge. There is no escaping the wrath of God by money, no purchasing a pardon with silver or gold and such corruptible things, for his justice cannot be bribed, nor any of the ministers of his justice, and in the day of the revelation of his wrath riches profit not (Prov. 11:4); and there is no escaping by rescue either, for though Job could muster ever so many to force him out of the hand of divine vengeance, God would not regard it, since none can deliver out of his hand. So the debate is genuine — is the verse a denial that riches and force can save, or a denial that crying and effort can? — while the point stands on either reading: against the wrath of God neither the purse nor the voice of man avails.
20:
Elihu warns Job against a longing the witnesses agree is the longing for death, though they first canvass other nights. The reformed John Gill ranges over the possibilities: the night literally — not, as with the thief or adulterer, for the covering of sin, of which Elihu had no suspicion in Job, but perhaps for retirement to muse, or for shelter from the hand of God, which no darkness can afford; or the night figuratively — either a night of calamity Job might wish upon his enemies, or, most likely, the night of death he had so often wished upon himself. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix that sense with a philologist's care: "pant not after the night," the night with the emphatic article, that shall take away peoples from their place — the syncopated form meaning "about to remove," and the phrase describing men fixed just where they are, without possibility of escape, deprived of being. And they draw the argument: if whole peoples are thus overtaken, how much less shall the individual escape? — yet Job presses on toward the tribunal of the terrible Judge instead of humbling himself under his hand.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, agrees the night is death, "as Job had done" in his earlier cries, or at least as his words might be understood, and corrects the number — for "people" read "peoples," that is, nations. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes the warning sharp and personal: the night of death, which Job had often desired, would leave him "irrecoverably gone"; let him take heed of his foolish and oft-repeated wish, lest God inflict it upon him in anger.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the last of the false refuges — no escaping the judgment of God by absconding, as a beaten army retreats under cover of night, for the darkness hides not from him (Ps. 139:11-12); and some, he notes, understand it of the night of death itself, the night by which men are cut off from their place, which Job had earnestly breathed after as the hireling longs for the shadow. But those who passionately wish for death, hoping to make it their shelter from God's wrath, may be sadly mistaken, for there are those whom wrath pursues into that night. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's death-wish, so far from being an escape, would only be the swiftest way into the very hand he sought to flee.
21:
The warning becomes a direct charge, and the witnesses agree on the iniquity in view while pressing its folly. The reformed John Gill takes "regard not iniquity" as a caution against showing any approbation of or desire after sin — and particularly against the sin Job had shown in his affliction, his impatience, his murmuring at God's dealings, his indecent speech; or, more narrowly, the evil of so earnestly desiring the night of death. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "take heed, incline not to evil, for this thou hast chosen rather than affliction," reading the closing verb as a deliberate preference — Job has chosen the evil of contending with God in place of the meek endurance of his trouble.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the whole into a warning against the death-wish as an affront to providence: it is sinful to entertain such longings, an insult to the God who sends affliction because he knows it best; Job has preferred death to affliction, thereby setting his own wisdom against the wisdom of God. Many in affliction long for death who are not prepared to meet God, Clarke adds; if he takes them at their wish they are ruined for ever, and the affliction that might have saved them is exchanged for the death that destroys. John Wesley reads the choice as Job's preferring "to quarrel with God, and censure his judgments, than quietly to submit to them."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry generalizes the lesson without softening it: let us never dare to think a favourable thought of sin, nor indulge it; Job had need of the caution, having chosen iniquity rather than affliction, that is, chosen rather to gratify his own pride and humour in contending with God than to mortify it by submission. And those who so choose make a foolish bargain, for there is more evil in the least sin than in the greatest affliction — sin is an evil, and only evil. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Elihu has laid his finger on a real temptation, the temptation to escape suffering by a sinful route, whether of despair, of murmuring, or of the longed-for grave, and that to take it is to prefer the worse thing to the better, the poison to the cure. The very framing of the verse, they observe, is a mercy in disguise: to be told that one has "chosen" iniquity is to be reminded that the choice may yet be unmade, and the affliction submitted to before the sin is finished.
22:
"Behold, God exalteth by his power; who teacheth like him?" — and the witnesses hear the speech lift, at this verse, from exhortation into the hymn of God's greatness that will carry to the chapter's end. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the change: the rest of Elihu's speech is splendidly eloquent, dilating on the power and majesty of God, and he seems to speak in contemplation of some gathering natural phenomenon — a tempest or whirlwind beginning to rise, the very storm out of which the LORD would at last answer (ch. 38:1) — which suggests the glorious imagery to come. The points, Ellicott says, are that God is the source of greatness, that there is no teacher like him, that he is absolute as well as almighty, and that he is unsearchable and eternal.

Over that second point the witnesses find a real crux of the Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch note that many, after the Septuagint's "sovereign," give the disputed word the sense "lord" or "ruler" — "who is a ruler like him?" — comparing the Aramaic and Arabic terms for lord; but they, with the Targum, Syriac, and Jerome, abide by the sense "teacher," both because the word has no etymological link with the term for lord and because it is peculiar to Elihu to represent God as a teacher, whether by dreams or by the discipline of affliction. So the line asks not who rules like God but who instructs like him.

That reading the other witnesses take up with delight. The reformed John Gill hears God exalting himself above all the praise of his creatures, and exalting his Son and his people. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns it on Job's case: "he has brought thee low, but he can raise thee up; thou art not yet out of the reach of his mercy; he knows what is best, and teaches thee how to suffer — why sin against his kindness? who can teach like him?" John Wesley presses the inference home: since none can work like God and none can teach like him, let Job not presume to teach him how to govern the world; none teaches with such authority, such condescension, such power, for he teaches by the Bible, the best book, and by his Son, the best Master. The witnesses do not finally divide; they weigh only whether the verse crowns God as ruler or as teacher, and, taking him for the teacher, draw the same rebuke to Job — that the pupil should not correct the master, nor the taught prescribe to him who alone teaches all.
23:
Two questions, both expecting the answer "none," carry the witnesses into the unaccountable sovereignty and flawless justice of God. The reformed John Gill takes the first: God teaches men his ways and prescribes the paths they should walk, but none can prescribe to him — none can teach him the path of judgment, or tell him whom to afflict, in what manner, or how long; all this he does according to his sovereign will and is not to be controlled, nor can any overlook his ways and call him to account. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "who hath appointed him his way, and who dare say, Thou doest iniquity?" — the two clauses together denying that any creature either directs God's course or convicts his conduct.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens both edges. Has God taken instructions from any man how to govern the world? And as for the second question, who can prove, in the whole compass of creation, that there is one thing imperfect, superabundant, or out of its place — one unrighteous, cruel, or unwise act in the course of divine providence? All the cunning and wickedness of man, Clarke says, have never been able to find the smallest flaw in the work of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the doctrine into three: God is an absolute sovereign, who exalts by his own power and not by any borrowed strength, having received his commission from none and being accountable to none; he is an incomparable teacher, for it is absurd to instruct him who is himself the fountain of light and knowledge — shall we light a candle to the sun? — and he is unexceptionably just in all his proceedings. Henry weighs the precise force of the last clause: not "who dares say, Thou hast wrought iniquity," for many do iniquity and tell God of his at their peril, but "who can say it" — who can say it with cause, and prove it? It is a maxim undoubtedly true, he concludes, that the King of kings can do no wrong; and the challenge to convict him, thrown open to the whole creation, has never in all the ages found a taker who could make the charge stick. The witnesses do not divide; they read the double question as the ground of all submission, that a God whose way none appointed and whose justice none can impeach is a God with whom it is not for Job, nor for any man, to contend.
24:
The command to "magnify his work" turns the witnesses to the works themselves and to a small question of how the last clause should read. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse the ground of submission: God's whole work is illustrious and conspicuous, and he does nothing mean; his visible works of nature, which we admire and in which we read his wisdom and power, are a good reason not to quarrel with his dealings in our own small affairs. The work of God is plain before our eyes, nothing more obvious — every man that has but half an eye may behold it afar off — and it ought to be not only justified as right but magnified as glorious, such as no creature could contrive; for the eternal power and Godhead of the Creator are clearly seen in the things that are made (Rom. 1:20), and there is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard (Ps. 19:3).

The reformed John Gill hears in "his work" both the works of creation and providence, magnified when men ascribe them to God and give him the glory, and, more particularly, the chastisement of his people — a work men magnify precisely when they bear it patiently and humble themselves under the mighty hand of God. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns it against Job's fretting: instead of quarrelling with his Maker, let him attentively survey the operation of his hands, the proofs of wisdom in the plan, of power in the production, of goodness in the end, and so magnify the work; John Wesley bids him "call to mind this thy duty," to magnify every work God does and condemn none, but adore all as done with admirable wisdom and justice.

Only the other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, raises the textual question, noting that some render the clause not "which men behold" but "whereof men sing," though he judges the former to suit the context best; Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, in fact render it "which men have sung," and add the following line, that all men delight in it while mortal man looks upon it from afar. So a small difference runs under the verse — whether the works of God are what men behold or what men have hymned — but the command is one on every reading: to magnify, and not to murmur at, the work of a God whose least act in providence is of a piece with the glory of the heavens.
25:
The universal visibility of God's work is the point, and the witnesses press how little excuse the plainness leaves. The reformed John Gill notes that the work is to be seen not only by the wise and learned but by the common people — whether one takes it of the works of creation, or of the afflictive providences of God in general, or of Job's afflictions in particular. The wesleyan-arminian voices sharpen it into an argument against unbelief. Adam Clarke: he who says he can examine the earth with a philosopher's eye and the heavens with an astronomer's, and yet cannot see in them a system of infinite skill and contrivance, must be ignorant of science or lying against his conscience, and is unworthy of confidence or respect. John Wesley: the power and wisdom and greatness of God are so manifest in all his works that all who are not stupid must see and acknowledge it, and the works are so great and conspicuous that they may be seen even at a great distance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose meditation on the divine work spans these verses, keeps the same note: the work of God is plain before our eyes, and every man — even those without the benefit of revelation — may behold it afar off, the heaven with all its lights and the earth with all its fruits declaring the work of Omnipotence, so that the eternal power and Godhead are understood by the things that are made.

And Wesley, catching the turn of the passage, observes that from this general visibility Elihu now proceeds to particular instances in the works of nature and common providence, his aim being to show that God is the first cause and supreme director of all creatures, whom therefore we ought to adore, and that it is presumption to prescribe to him in his special dealings with men when even the common operations of the clouds are so mysterious and unaccountable. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the hinge between doctrine and demonstration: having asserted that God's work is great and to be magnified, Elihu appeals to the plainest evidence — that it lies open to every eye, near and far, learned and simple — and prepares to lead Job out of doors, as it were, to the clouds and the rain and the thunder, that the wonders a man cannot fathom in the sky may teach him not to demand an account of the wonders he cannot fathom in his own life.
26:
"Behold, God is great, and we know him not," Elihu says, and the witnesses take the confession of ignorance as the summit of the doctrine. The reformed John Gill unfolds the greatness first — God great in power and wisdom, in truth and faithfulness, in love and mercy, and great too, on one reading of the word, as "much" or "many," in the plurality of his persons, Father, Son, and Spirit, in the fulness of his perfections, and in the multitude of his thoughts and works and blessings, so many they cannot be reckoned. But the weight of the verse for Gill falls on the "we know him not": we know that he is, but not what he is; we know what he is not, but not what he is; we know in part, but not in perfection.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reduces the verse to three propositions, each a foundation for endless meditation: "God is great" — he is omnipotent; "we know him not" — he is unsearchable; and "neither can the number of his years be searched out" — he is eternal; and these, Clarke says, are too profound and sublime to need paraphrase. John Wesley presses the last clause: God is eternal, as in his being so in all his counsels, which must therefore be infinitely above the comprehension of short-lived men — the very point Elihu is driving at, that a creature of a day should not arraign the everlasting God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers it up: the streams of being and power should lead us to the fountain, and God is great — great in power, for he is omnipotent and independent; great in himself, great in all his works; and therefore we know him not, for the number of his years cannot be searched out, since he is a Being without beginning, succession, or period, ever the same, the great "I AM." Keil and Delitzsch, of the grammatical-historical school, render the couplet "Behold, God is exalted — we know him not entirely; the number of his years, it is unsearchable," and note that the very word for "unsearchable" is one that otherwise appears only in the later, Aramaic-tinged Hebrew. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the deliberate crown of the argument, a knowledge that ends in confessed ignorance — not that God is unknown, for his greatness is visible to every eye, but that he is never known to the bottom, and the eternity of his counsels is the last and best reason why a mortal should adore and not dispute.
27:
"He maketh small the drops of water," Elihu begins, and with the first of his instances the witnesses enter the wonder of the rain. The reformed John Gill notes that Elihu, like Eliphaz before him, opens with rain — a common phenomenon, known in every age and country, yet with something in it beyond man's comprehension, so that the design is to convince Job of his folly in searching out the causes of God's providence when the common works of nature lie out of his reach. The words, Gill adds, are variously rendered — "he restrains the drops of rain," withholding it in drought, or "he draws up" the drops, exhaling them by the sun's heat out of the earth and sea.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as a plain account of evaporation, preferring to translate "he exhales" — God detaches the smallest particles from the surface of the waters to form the clouds, those reservoirs for the watering of the earth; and he draws the moral that God is seen in little things as in great, the inconceivably small and the stupendously great being equally the work of Omnipotence. The rain, he notes, is "according to the vapour thereof," proportioned to the quantity evaporated and condensed into cloud. John Wesley marks the wisdom of the measure: God so orders it that the waters in the clouds do not fall at once in spouts, which would ruin the earth, but by degrees and in drops, according to the proportion of vapours the sun has drawn up — a constant rotation by which rain is made of vapour and resolved again into vapour.

The grammatical-historical witnesses keep to the mechanism. Keil and Delitzsch describe the wondrous origin of rain, the drops of water distilling as rain "in connection with its mist"; Charles Ellicott hears the first beginnings of the tempest — "he maketh small," or draweth up by exhalation, and "they pour down rain from his vapour," the water first absorbed and then distilled and poured down. Matthew Henry, of the puritan-evangelical school, adds the theology the mechanism serves: the clouds pour down according to the vapour they draw up, so just are the heavens to the earth; and every good gift being from above, from the Father of the rain as of lights, the common shower should teach us to look up. The witnesses do not divide; they read the small, measured raindrop as a parable of the God who dispenses even his mercies by exact weight, too wise to drown and too kind to withhold.
28:
The clouds that distil their gathered water "upon man" draw the witnesses to the bounty of the gift and, in one ancient voice, to the character of the man who preaches it. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great pauses over Elihu himself at this turn in the speech: whoever would gain knowledge from the mighty words of the arrogant must guard against catching their pride along with their eloquence, for to hear such men is to enter a garden and pluck roses among thorns — we must cull what is sweet-scented and avoid what pricks. Elihu, being both learned and arrogant, yields at one moment something fragrant and at another something that wounds; and here, Gregory observes, he abandons the low ground of morality and rises to the heights of prophecy, for even an unworthy person may receive holy words by the spirit of prophecy without thereby attaining a holy nature — as Saul prophesied among the prophets (1 Sam. 10:11), and as the dumb ass spoke with man's voice and rebuked the madness of the prophet (2 Pet. 2:16), yet neither was changed in nature by the words they uttered.

The reformed John Gill keeps to the rain and its liberality: the clouds distil not upon the persons of men, which they take pains to shun, but upon the fields of men, for their profit and advantage, letting the water down in an easy and plentiful manner and upon an abundance of lands — though sometimes, he notes, rain falls upon the wilderness where no man is. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the mechanism: in proportion to the evaporation is the mass of suspended vapour, and in proportion to that the rain that falls in its several forms; and he records the striking addition the Septuagint makes to the verse — "the rains descend, and the clouds overshadow multitudes of men... at the contemplation of these things, is not thy mind transported, and thy heart ready to part from thy body?"

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out why the text says the rain falls "upon man": though God causes it to rain in the wilderness where no man is, special respect is had to man, to whom the creatures are made serviceable and from whom the tribute of praise is required; and among men he causes his rain to fall upon the just and upon the unjust (Matt. 5:45), so abundantly that the shower is called the river of God which is full of water (Ps. 65:9). The witnesses do not divide; they read the distilling cloud as pure liberality — a gift measured in small drops yet poured on multitudes, falling on the deserving and undeserving alike — and, with Gregory, take even the flawed preacher of it as proof that God can send true words through an unworthy vessel, as he sends the rain on field and wilderness together.
29:
From the falling rain Elihu lifts his eyes to the spread canopy above it, and the witnesses own the mystery he presses. The reformed John Gill marvels at the spreading of a cloud that begins no bigger than a man's hand and in a little time covers the whole heavens (1 Kings 18:44): none can understand or describe by what means so small a thing is so prodigiously stretched, nor how the clouds, spread to such an extent, are poised and balanced in the air to keep their place as long as God pleases; they serve at once as a pavilion around him and as an umbrella for men against the heat. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enlarges the same wonder: the vapour, seemingly at the mercy of every wind and current, might be driven to the deserts or dropped back into the sea, yet the providence of God so manages it that every part of the arable earth receives its supply; and by "the noise of his tabernacle" he understands the whole firmament, the atmospheric expanse where the Almighty seems to dwell, the noise being the blowing of tempests and the rattling of thunder.

John Wesley, of the same school, keeps the two wonders together: how a cloud no bigger than a man's hand suddenly spreads over the whole heavens, and how the clouds come to be so gathered and condensed as to bring forth thunder and lightning — the thunder being the noise of what is often called God's tent or tabernacle. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the picture of the spreading: it describes how the clouds are heaped up one upon another like mountains in the sky when the storm gathers; and the second clause he would render "the thunderings of his pavilion," comparing the dark waters and thick clouds of the psalmist's theophany (Ps. 18:11-12).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the argument Elihu intends: if we cannot understand the spreading of the clouds that we daily see — how they come to be stretched out and poised as a curtain over the earth — shall we pretend to understand the reasons and methods of God's judicial proceedings with men, whose characters and cases are so various? The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the canopy overhead, so common and so unaccountable, is set here as a rebuke to curiosity — that a man baffled by a cloud has no standing to demand the secrets of providence, and that the thunder of God's tabernacle should hush the questioner rather than embolden him.
30:
The verse flashes with light and plunges to the sea-bed, and the witnesses divide over both the light and where it is spread. The reformed John Gill offers several senses: the light of the sun, whereby the clouds are dispersed and blotted out — an emblem of the forgiveness of sin, a clear shining after rain; or the lightning that bursts from the dark cloud and seems to set it in flames; or, with Cocceius, "he spreads the light about himself," God clothing himself with light as with a garment and dwelling in light inaccessible; or he spreads it "upon man," causing his sun to rise on just and unjust, or upon the earth, as when light was first commanded to shine out of darkness. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the light as lightning — "he throweth forth from it his flash" — the sudden rarefaction of the air whence the thunder proceeds; and "covereth the bottom of the sea" he takes of God's absolute control over the deep, which is as much under his hand as the atmosphere with all its vapours and fires. John Wesley agrees the light is the lightning, fitly called God's light because God only can kindle it, the cloud being the candlestick in which he sets it up, and its reach so far and deep that it pierces even to the bottom of the sea.

The grammatical-historical witnesses read the sea more subtly. Charles Ellicott takes "his light" for the lightning that flashes from the cloud, and "the roots of the sea" — not the bottom — for the clouds themselves, composed of the drops of water exhaled from the sea, which the lightning, or God, has covered. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "He spreadeth his light over himself, and the roots of the sea he covereth," siding with Cocceius against the "upon it" of the Authorized Version.

So the differences are real and several: is the "light" the sun that clears the sky or the lightning that splits the cloud? and does God spread it "upon it," the cloud, "about himself," or upon man and earth? and is the covered deep the literal bottom of the sea or the cloud-roots drawn up from it? The witnesses do not resolve every point, but they meet in the awe the verse means to raise — a God who wraps himself in light, hurls it to the depths, and holds both the flash above and the abyss below in a single hand.
31:
The same clouds serve God as both scourge and storehouse, and the witnesses read the double office. The reformed John Gill catalogues the judgments God executes by the clouds and what issues from them — rain, hail, wind, thunder, lightning: he drowned the old world by a deluge from the deep and the windows of heaven (Gen. 7:11), smote the Egyptians with a storm of hail (Exod. 9:23), cast down hailstones on the Canaanites, rained fire and brimstone on Sodom (Gen. 19:24), and discomfited the Philistines with thunder; yet by the same clouds he shows mercy, as the following clause declares. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line plainly, "for thereby he judgeth peoples, he giveth food in abundance," the two clauses setting judgment and provision side by side.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the mercy at length. God makes storms and tempests, hurricanes and tornadoes, drought and flood the instruments of his justice to punish rebellious nations; yet through the same, as instruments, he provides for all: storms agitate and purify the lower air, dispersing noxious vapours that would otherwise stagnate into a deadly mass, and by dews and rains and snows and winds he fructifies the earth, so that every living thing is filled with plenteousness. Clarke pauses to reject a proposed rendering of the second clause, "he passeth sentence amain," which he can find in none of the versions and which loses the fine idea of the common translation. John Wesley keeps the balance: by thunder and lightning and rain God executes his judgments against ungodly people, and by the same clouds provides plentiful showers dropping fatness on the earth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott ties the "them" back to the rain-clouds and drops of the previous verse: by them God "judgeth peoples," whether by withholding the rain in famine or sending it in excess to chastise nations with inundation, and by them he "giveth meat in abundance" when he sends it in due measure on the earth. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sums the whole: the produce of the clouds is sometimes a great terror and at other times a great favour to the earth — storms and floods that destroy the fruits, or the rain that drops fatness on the pastures — and this difference must be resolved into the providence that orders it. The witnesses do not divide; they read the cloud as the very emblem of a God whose one hand deals death and bread, judgment and harvest, according to the deserts of nations and the counsels of his will.
32:
Here the witnesses meet one of the chapter's real cruxes, for a single Hebrew word turns the verse two opposite ways. The reformed John Gill keeps the Authorized sense: God "covereth the light," whether the lightning hid in the dark cloud until it bursts out, or the light of the sun obscured when clear waters formed into cloud darken it — as in the long tempest that hid sun and stars from Paul and his shipmates many days (Acts 27:20). John Wesley reads it the same way: with thick and black clouds spread over the whole heavens God covers the light of the sun, the cloud a veil he interposes between the sun and the earth.

But the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the verse "extraordinary" and hard, and reports the rival constructions: the Vulgate and most versions have "in his hands he hideth the light" — by the hollow of his hands he conceals the light, the fountain of light, the sun; Mr. Good has "he brandisheth the blaze athwart the concave"; and Clarke himself, unwilling to lay a correcting hand on so difficult a text, half suspects an allusion to eclipses, God covering the sun's body with the hollow of his hand and then removing it to re-illuminate the earth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the crux to a decision. The word rendered "clouds," he says, really means hands, and there is no good reason to take it otherwise; the verse should read "he covereth the lightning with his hands, and giveth it a charge that it strike the mark" — the figure being that of a man who grasps a stone or bolt, takes aim, and hurls it, a very fine image, and one the Authorized Version has obscured with its five inserted words. So the debate is genuine and sharp: does God "with clouds cover the light" of the sun, drawing a veil between it and the earth, or does he "cover the lightning in his hands" and aim it, like a marksman, at its target? The one reading makes the verse a picture of the darkened sky, the other of the aimed thunderbolt. The witnesses do not settle it; they leave the word poised between cloud and palm, agreeing only that whichever it be, the light — of the sun or of the lightning — is wholly at the command of God, covered and uncovered, loosed and aimed, at his sovereign will.
33:
The chapter ends in thunder, on a verse the witnesses call one of the hardest in the book, and they divide over almost every word. The reformed John Gill takes the plainer sense: the noise — the sound of the clouds, or of the wind, or of the thunder — is a presage that rain is coming, showing concerning it before it falls. John Wesley reads it the same way and completes the couplet: the thunder gives notice of the approaching rain, and the cattle too, by a strange instinct, show concerning the coming change, seeking shelter when the weather is near to turn.

But the grammatical-historical witnesses hear the verse announcing not the rain but God. Keil and Delitzsch reject the rendering that makes the word mean "his friend," and take it as "his noise" — his thunder gives tidings concerning him, announces him. Charles Ellicott, owning the verse "extremely difficult" and its sense "very uncertain," translates the first clause "the crash of the thunder declareth concerning him": it is God's voice and speaks of him; the last clause he finds almost unintelligible, the words meaning perhaps "cattle even concerning a goer-up" — so that the thunder-crash tells the very cattle of him who goeth up on high, even the beasts showing by their terror that the thunder speaks to them of God. All nature, on this reading, shares the awe the thunder wakes.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, unhappy with the received translation, offers a bolder one of his own: "its loud noise shall proclaim concerning him — a magazine of wrath against iniquity," reading the last word not as "cattle" but as a treasury, and hearing in the thunder the artillery of the skies, at whose voice every wicked man trembles as at the voice of God. So the differences are many — whether the noise tells of the coming rain or announces God himself; whether the last clause speaks of cattle sensing the storm, of cattle terrified before the God who rises, or of a stored-up wrath against sin — and the witnesses cannot resolve them, for the Hebrew, they confess, will hardly yield a settled sense. Yet they meet at the last in the general truth all the readings carry: that the thunder is heard as the audible voice of God, before which the earth and its creatures alike bow, and that Elihu ends his speech, as the next chapter will continue it, by pointing Job away from his own case to the storm now gathering — the very tempest out of which the LORD will presently answer him.
